system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
[person] was admitted to the hospital on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours in a ward. She is a 60-year-old female cleaner from [address] with incomplete high school education. Her estimated weight is 60 kg, predicted weight 57 kg, and height 164 cm. She has liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver). During this stay, she had septic shock (severe infection causing low BP) from a lung source, acute respiratory failure (breathing difficulty), low BP, and decreased consciousness. Blood tests showed Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. She also had acute kidney injury (kidney stress) which resolved. Her liver condition caused pleural effusion (fluid around lungs) and ascites (fluid in belly), requiring paracentesis (draining belly fluid) and thoracentesis (draining lung fluid).

On 09/19, belly fluid tests showed low protein and albumin. Lung fluid tests showed it was a transudate (fluid from pressure, not infection). On 09/23, 700 ml of lung fluid was drained. On 10/06, 1000 ml was drained. On 10/10, 1000 ml was drained. On 10/15, 1000 ml was drained. Before this admission, she was seen on 02/09/2022 for massive ascites and breathing trouble. Her diuretics (water pills) were increased to Furosemide 40 mg twice daily and Spironolactone 50 mg daily. Paracentesis drained 4.1 liters that day. On 13/09, another paracentesis drained 1.4 liters. She was referred from emergency care on 18/09/2022 with low oxygen levels, confusion, and blue skin. She was intubated (breathing tube inserted) and sedated.

In the hospital, she was treated for possible lung infection or sepsis. Ceftriaxone (antibiotic) was started. Tests ruled out belly infection. Lung fluid was drained. A POCUS (quick ultrasound) showed lung lines and thickening, supporting sepsis. On 09/24, antibiotics changed to Levofloxacin and Oxacillin after blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was done to check for heart valve infection. On 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to Meropenem and Oxacillin due to worsening inflammation. She improved, was removed from the breathing tube on 10/03, and stopped oxygen on 10/13. Antibiotics ended on 10/08. She stayed longer for nursing care, pressure injury treatment, and fluid management.

Her history includes liver cirrhosis diagnosed in 2021, diabetes, high BP, and anxiety. She has had previous biopsies showing liver fibrosis and fatty liver. She has esophageal varices (swollen veins in food pipe). She is allergic to Dipyrone. She used to smoke and drink beer but stopped. Her home medicines include Insulin, Glifage XR (for sugar), Simvastatin (for cholesterol), Losartan (for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (water pill), Sertraline (for mood), Gabapentin (for nerve pain), Calcium/Vitamin D, Amitriptyline (for pain/sleep), Propranolol (for BP/varices), Omeprazole (for stomach acid), Furosemide, and Spironolactone.

During the stay, she had a nasoenteral tube (feeding tube), central venous access (IV line in neck), and urinary catheter (urine tube). Blood cultures showed Staphylococcus aureus initially, then other harmless bacteria. Lung and belly fluid cultures were negative. A CT scan showed lung fluid and heart enlargement. The heart ultrasound showed normal pumping strength but some valve leakage.

At discharge, her diuretic doses will be adjusted while monitoring kidneys. She will continue to have belly and lung fluid drained as needed. Oxygen support will be reduced slowly. The feeding tube will be removed if she eats well. Pressure sores on her back and hips will be treated. She has a follow-up appointment on 18/01. The family has been informed about the seriousness of her condition. A decision was made together not to perform new invasive procedures.
